speaker: Speaker 1
words: We should tie all of that dead into a bound so we won't get any interruptions. Well, I'm Isabelle Miller and I'm here at Mrs. Bell's house. And you are, your first name is?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Eva May.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Eva May Bell. And we're just talking here. And I had a few questions to ask and Eva's decided she'll answer the ones she wants to. And I'll just start out in order to start the discussion. Remembering your childhood being a girl, do you feel you were treated any differently than your brothers when you grew up?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Probably favored because I was the oldest and the only girl and there were four boys.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So you were valued, I think, for being the older girl.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I would say. And yet, of course, responsibilities were placed on me that weren't on the boys, too. So that'd be a little hard to say just that I was favored either, but I got to go places my brothers didn't get to go at all. I get to go stay at my grandmother's because I am at my age. When I was working in Michigan, I got to go with him to Tico and the boys stayed home.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So you felt pretty good about being a girl.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, I did.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you, you felt like you had more opportunities because of your age?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I did, yes.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And you must have been pretty responsible and your family could, uh... Is that Mrs. Larson? Okay, we've been joined by Mrs. Larson who's going to talk with us on this same subject. Your first name is what? Patsy. Patsy Larson. And I'm going, since Mrs. Bell has kind of started answering that question about how she felt being a girl, she can talk, think a little bit more about that while Mrs. Patsy Larson talks about how she felt when she was growing up. I didn't give it too much consideration that I was a girl. I mean, it was just one of the things that it was. Did you have any brothers? Yes, I had an older brother. Did you feel like he was privileged or you felt... Not particularly. I think he was because he was older. More because of his difference in age. But not because he was a boy. How about chores you did around the house? I think it was probably work. You were... Did you work mostly in the house helping your mother? Mostly. You were satisfied with it? Yes, I was. I didn't feel that he was way above me. How about when it came time to growing up? Did you decide to get married or was it expected of you? Oh, I decided to get married. I don't think it was expected. I don't think it was expected. How about you, Eva Mae?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Same thing.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Your parents said it was pretty open that you could do whatever you wanted to.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, but they still didn't want me to because they wanted me to go on to school. I didn't want to go on to school.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: They wanted you to go to high school or college or what was it?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, yes. I haven't finished high school yet. They want me to go on to finish high school. At least probably go on to college, but they definitely want me to go on through high school.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Why did you decide to get married?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I just wasn't interested in school and I couldn't see any advantage of it. I still don't particularly, in my case, I don't think it was what I wanted to do for my purpose in life. I don't think that that would help me a bit.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And you all along had planned to be a housewife and a mother?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That was my big ambition in life. And you weren't doing anything in school that held my interest? Mm-hmm.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Was that true for you or how did you feel about school? I didn't particularly like school. I went to school because I was expected to go to school, but not because I liked it. Did you finish high school? I finished high school. Well, you were glad. Yes, I was very glad when I finished. And had you always wanted to get married? Yes, I think so. I always wanted a family. They go together. That was just what you grew up with? Could you have gone? I could have gone to college if I wanted to. So clearly that was your choice? I think now I'm sorry that I didn't go. Why do you say that? Because I think college broadened your outlook on life and you have more experiences. But you saw it more as just postponing marriage. You would have married anyway? Eventually, yes. Yes, I wanted to marry. But going to college would have given you more of a broader, just more... It would have given me a broader outlook on life and more experiences. Would you think you'd marry the same man? That's a good question. Maybe what your opportunities would have been. That's hindsight. How about you? You wouldn't have considered college if you had to do over again?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, I still wouldn't. I do think getting married too young... I was 18 when she wasn't really too young, I guess. But in my case as far as a college education, I think... Because you miss a lot, you know, growing up. Because when you get out of school and you go right into responsibilities of marriage... Of course, we were married four years before we had any children and then adopted one. So I think a lot of that depends too on how... We went through a depression. So I don't... as far as my answer, I think you can educate yourself. Self-education, I think. But then there's a lot you miss being with young people, as she says, when you don't go to college. There's a lot that you do miss. But for me, I don't regret a minute of it. I'd do the same thing right over. And marry the same man. Couldn't have been pampered so much.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay then. And do you have children? You do. How many? I have eight. Eight children. And you adopted one more?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Just one.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You just raised the one. And you found you couldn't have children. Yeah. Were you sorry about this?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, yes, we should have had two. We were satisfied with just the one. It was all we could... time, that's all we thought about. Because my health wasn't good either. Because I had asthma even then. And I just didn't feel that I really could take two. Because we wished Atherton could have two. And I adopted the other.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That's another story. And you were telling me before I started recording that you thought that was probably the most worthwhile thing, a woman.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I do. Because... I do. You bring children up and they contribute to the world. And if you do a good job, I don't think there's anything more worthwhile.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So in effect, the work you're doing through other children is the way you contribute to the world and your community.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Right. And this is more or less the way I feel about my study school class for 27 years. Working with children. I love it. Every minute of it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Would you agree with that about women's contribution? Yes, I would. Would you want to add anything to that? I can't think of anything right now. I wish you do. And I said, was this traumatic for you not to have children of your own?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No. It really wasn't. Perhaps... I don't even know if we ever adopted one. This was a nephew. And we thought... I just sat there and couldn't stand it because he was arrogant to give him to the children's home. And I just couldn't stand it. I wanted him so badly. And my husband walked here to Moscow to find out we didn't have a car. It was Depression time, see? And he made the trip, walked over there to see if we could adopt him. And we did.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Your sister died?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, my husband's brother and his wife separated. Oh. So it was on my husband's side. But we thoroughly enjoyed that child, I'll tell you. We really enjoyed him. As I look back, I'm sure that we should have had somebody for him. I think more for his sake, maybe even than for our own, because too many times you expect too much of them when they're an only child.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, feeling the way you did then about women's main contribution being through raising children, what would you have done if you hadn't had him?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: This I don't know. You know? It's something that's just kind of like hindsight. You don't know what you... I don't know what we'd have done.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But you were feeling pretty good about yourself, what you were doing. You didn't hint that you...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, it was Depression times and you had to just scrape, you know. And he went out and went to Lester's when we adopted him in order to give us food and clothing to keep going. And of course we didn't know anything. We were married in 1930 and this was 1934 that we adopted him. And it was pretty hard going. So then as time went on, I don't know how it would have gone. But our whole lives just kind of revolved around him and yet we didn't... see, didn't give him a lot of... I mean, he had strict rules and all this. Now, on the other hand, he was disciplined. It wasn't like he was just giving his way and everything that he wanted or anything like this. Probably as much as if he'd had brothers and sisters.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That's hard. When were you married? I was married in 1947. And you've had eight children. I've actually had ten. Two of my children died. Did you want that many children? Yes, I did. So you were pleased every time you had another one? Well, yes, I guess so. You'd expected to have a lot of children. Oh, I wanted a lot of children. There were only two in my family. I felt that I was always envious of the people that did have children. And I'm glad that I lived at that time instead of now when you're supposed to only have two. Do you feel pressure now? Do you feel women now are kind of discouraged from having more children? Yes, I do. I think they're quite pressured not to have more children. And if you do have more... Like, my husband and I, my older daughter went to college and she had a friend. And they asked, how many children do your parents have? And she said they have eight. And this kid looked at her and he said, well, they should be fine. That was the attitude. And I think this is the attitude that the young women have now if they want children. So it sounds like they don't have a choice to make for themselves. Well, not actually that. So there's some... They're discriminated against. They do have a large family. Even if they have them because they want them. That's a pretty personal decision.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Okay. Well, let's go back to...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You got married just because you wanted to. Right. And you really wanted to. Because you planned that all along. How did your parents... You said something about your parents tried to discourage you.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, they tried to discourage me. They wanted us to wait.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Because you were so young.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, I was only 18. See, I didn't start school until I was eight years old. Because I was little and we lived a long way from school and I had to walk alone. I had to wait until my brother was old enough to come with me. And this made me a little late. And maybe this also is... We went to school in one little school with eight grades and one teacher. And sixth and seventh and eighth graders taught the first graders. And the first two years I went through three grades and I didn't get them. And when I got older, this made schooling very hard for me. I went into town to school and the teacher said, You have absolutely no foundation. And this may be one reason why I didn't care for school, either. Because one of my brothers who said he played all through high school, took him five years, now he's a psychologist over at Kent School. So this probably had a lot to do with whether I liked or disliked it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Where did he go? Did he go to the same school?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: The same school, but at that time we had two teachers and four grades.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So he just got a better education.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Right. He had a good start, I mean, a better chance. He didn't like school, he played all through his eighth grade and through high school. And still now, then he went into the Navy and then he became a psychiatrist. He's a psychologist, that's what he is.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Were your parents, it was okay with them when you got married? Were they pleased with you? No, they weren't. Oh, what was their objection? They thought I was too young and they wanted me to go on to school. And they thought my husband was too old for me, he's nine years older than I am. We know. And that was upsetting to the family. Yes. You, you remember this, you've watched this family. Right. You've been neighbors all these years. That's interesting. Did you, was she a friend? Did you come to her?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No. No. I was married, see, we had, oh, my bub was born in 33. So I see he was eight years old by the time she got married.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But you just observed this.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, because your mother and I were real good friends.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You heard from her mother, probably. Yeah. Did you sympathize with her mother? Well, no, not particularly. I don't think Patsy said anything.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I could understand Patsy, though, you boy.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you tell her mother anything?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I don't think that your mother said too much, really.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: She didn't ask, really. There was very little to say. No.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You're just not the only one.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: There was a lot of facts. Where did you go when you were little?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We went to Portland, to the Hitchin' Post. We went to Moskvin, got married, and my folks knew it, and everything, you know.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So you alone, too?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: So we didn't go out, no.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: No, well, it was kind of just... Yeah. We didn't go have a big wedding. Privately, you mean.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah. Well, my aunt and uncle, two aunts and an uncle went with us, and folks knew all about it and everything. We'd come back the next day, and then they had a chivalry, and all my relatives were there and everything, so...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: They had a chivalry? Yeah. That's something to describe. Right. That's what I'd like to hear about.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, we came back about, oh, 6.30 in the afternoon, I guess. All my relatives were still there, and it just began to get dark, and all the cars came up the hill, and it was quite a steep hill to get up there. And they started blowing their horns before they even got there. And then they made all the noise they could make, standing around hollering, and then you'd take out candy and cigars.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You had to be prepared for it.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You had to be prepared. We came from Spokane well prepared.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Was this your folks' house? Did I miss that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: To my folks' house.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You were back there, and all your friends came from all over the community. Right. And then you passed out cigars and candy. Yeah. Was there any unpleasant experiences in this one? No. They didn't cart you off, or your husband off, or any of the adverts and things like that. So this was a happy gathering. Right. And everything. So this is a pleasant occasion. You should have a welcome back to the community. Yes.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We've lived here ever since.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is this the house?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: For three months, no. We've done all, there was nothing here when we came here. Except for three months we lived in Knopf River. But all the rest of our lives have been lived right in this community. All of my life, since I was born, I have lived in this community. How long is that? Sixty-three years, in the last December.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Sixty-three years.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Sixty-three years in a month. And my husband was born at Colville. He came here in 1929.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is he farming?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, he's retired now.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, he's retired, yeah. But he did work as what?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: He worked at the mill. Well, we own a farm, but, and he farmed for seven years. But he also worked at the mill. To pay for everything, and buy your machinery and everything on these little farms. And it wasn't clear, everything was trees. We had to get stumps in here to move in one house, one 14 by 18 foot room, and then we'd build everything around it. It started out as what was part of that living room, and everything has been added on since.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: As you could afford it, and had time to do it.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Right, he did everything himself.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So it's really a house that grew. Right.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And then he's done, well, of course, we've hired some, a little bit of wiring there first.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you help with any of it?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yes, I've helped a few, found a few nails, and of course, I've done a lot of painting and everything. But the thing I helped with a lot of it, I couldn't do it. I would like to.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But you fixed the mills.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yes.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That was the... Right. So that he could spend time...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Like the thrashing beat we used to have, you know, we had a thrashing machine first, before we had a combine. And then there'd be old 14, 15 men come, and there'd be the neighbor, we'd go from house to house, each one cooking, and these were great experiences.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, tell us about those. I haven't heard about anything like that.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, you'd bake pies, lots of pies, and all kinds of desserts, everything imaginable. Potatoes and gravy and meat were the most important thing of all. And then your vegetables.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Even though it's hot weather.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Hot weather didn't make any difference. How hot it was, and you'd cook this over a wood stove and perspire to open up a window. But then all this baking, and then there'd be about, usually about three or four women.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And they'd get...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Neighbors. Right, neighbors. And then we wanted to go, like, to their house, and they'd come to my house, and then when we got to my house, we'd go to the other house. And wherever it'd be, this is what they'd do.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Now, the men working were all neighbors, too. Right. Did they hire anybody else to help?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Just neighbors.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Just cooperation. Right.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It was the same thing in the hay. They'd do the same thing.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How did they ever... I've often wondered who determined who went first. So bad weather came, and somebody...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, in all prior this time, it was a shared... One time we had a combine with four men. Four of my husband and three neighbors, all on the same machine. So just whatever grain would be ready. Now, some people would live up a little higher, and their grain would be ready first. And we're down here where it's low, and part of ours would be lower later than the others.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So they just determined this among them. Right.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And sometimes they'd start up in the lower, up in the higher place, and just come on down. They'd pick whichever one they'd come to first, rather than move the machinery up over a hill and go miles all the way and then come back. If the grain was ready, they'd just take it as if they'd come to it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And the machinery was owned cooperatively?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, it was that combine. And the thrashing machine... Yeah, the thrashing machine, we owned ourselves.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But the women, when this time came, they just got together and they... Did you have telephones?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, they had a telephone. We didn't have, but most of them did have. And you could call her if you didn't, you just go out and tell them, you know. And more of the men were working together, and going, well, we'll be down to your place at such and such a time. And then we'd just get together. Just automatically, this is something we just did.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And how did you determine who made, bought, and the food?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, usually the... Of course, everything would be at your home. If you had apple pies where it was, it would be at your home.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: If they were harvesting at your place, then that's where the men ate. Right. And the other neighbor women came in and helped to prepare.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: This is what they...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Was it your food?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: My food. Your food? No, they would bring food. They'd usually just come to help, to help you to get it cooked. And do the dishes up afterwards.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And then they'd go home and work on their own places.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And you'd have to heat your water on the stove. All this kind of thing, because you had to go outside and get the water. My husband would pump all the water and bring it home to the house and have plenty for me, you know, so that I'd have it. So I never heard of having to carry water. But this is what you'd do. And then you'd heat the water on the wood stove and cook your meals. And afterwards you'd have to heat the water to do the dishes, and the dishes.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What time in the morning did you get up then?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: About 4.30, 5 o'clock. About 4.30 usually.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How about how many people would sit down at the table then?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: At least about 14.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Would that be the men first? Usually the men. The men would eat first and go back out to the field.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, and then we would usually eat.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: It was a nice social occasion.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yeah.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: We really enjoyed it.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We really enjoyed it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Because after that work was done, you kind of relaxed.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I even enjoyed talking about it, thinking about it, you know, thinking back, it brings pleasant memories.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: It's kind of a thing that's a little bit like a family thing. It's lost now. It's harder for women to get together. A lot harder. Did you have any experiences like that? No, I didn't. So that since the war, people could own their own machinery, and do they harvest their own little pots now, or how is that? Well, most people do.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: So they don't need to cooperate. No.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But they need more money invested in the machinery, each one.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: See, we sold what machinery we had, so that our farm was leased out. So of course the people come here and do our haying or our combine, whatever, or just home, maybe two or three in the family that do it. Because one will drive a truck, and one runs the combine. Sometimes there's two drivers.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But now each farmer needs more money, more investment, so he can do it himself, and we've lost this nice social cooperative feeling.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Like our community club that we used to have is as high as 30 people in it. Now there's seven of us.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Where does your husband work? My husband can't get on a plane right now. We have a farm, though. He works at a small sawmill. And it's a seasonal unemployment, or is it a result of the housing? Yeah, it's seasonal. Ordinarily, he's a sawyer. And when we were first married, he was a sawyer. That means going down the tree, the first one. Yes. Did they have power saws then, or did he use combs? They used power saws. Was this... Did you feel pretty secure, and he'd make a good living for you? No. I felt secure in that he would make me a good living, but I didn't feel secure in the fact that he'd come home alive every night. Oh, that's something else, isn't it? That would be from accidents that were pretty frequent. Yes. Was this an objection? Did your parents object to your marrying a man in this? No. At that time, he was a carpenter. Oh, I see. And was more money in this other or...? Oh, yes. It was a very well-paid job. Because it was dangerous. Yeah. And it probably wasn't your idea that he'd take this? No. No, definitely not. Did he enjoy it, or was it just to get more money? Oh, he enjoyed it. That was a wonderful job. And how long did he stay with it? He stayed with it until seven years ago, and he hurt his foot. A tree broke off the man's foot. So he was in it quite a while before anything happened to him. So he broke his back and cut his head two or three times. Assorted things like that, but nothing really serious. Ha ha ha ha! Anyway, he came out alive. And then after he hurt his foot, when he went to work in the mill? He wasn't able to walk around in the woods anymore, because most of the logging is done on the steep hills by the mountains. But he did it partly because he enjoyed it. I would say completely because he enjoyed it. You weren't putting pressure on him to earn more money, in spite of the fact you were having more children. No, I was not, because I was putting pressure on him to quit, because I wanted him to come home every night.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: In one piece.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, what happens in a situation like that? Obviously, he didn't pay attention to you. Obviously. What was his... did you suggest to him? Well, actually, I told him what I thought, but it was his life. I had no right to tell him what he was to do. That's the way you feel. That was okay, he made the decision. I wasn't happy about it, but it was his decision and his life. Was there anything said about, what, if you come home an invalid and I have to... No. ...deal with that? No. So, it still was his decision. You live with whatever. You adjusted to whatever he decided to do. Okay, then. This is very interesting. I enjoy hearing this. And did he want many children, too? I don't really know. When we were married, we wanted five. Did you talk about having five? Yeah. You determined it. And then I had problems. Our first baby died at birth. And then I had two miscarriages. And then we had our four children, and we didn't really plan on any more. And then we had our son, and he died. And then we really realized how really important your children are. And became more precious. And I wanted another baby, so we had another baby. And there was a five-year difference between those two. And he was more at the lonesome, and I had another baby. He had their company. And then we wanted a girl, and we decided to gamble. And we had any of them. You won. And then we had another boy. We had six boys, and I had two girls. Well, obviously you wanted the most, and it was okay with him. Well, he didn't deal too violently.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, he's from a family of 13, and she's from a family of two.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So he could deal with a lot of children. Anyway, it didn't bother me. I guess it's just what I was tasked with life. But you're just... everybody's happy with you. Oh, I think so. What do you do for rec... you can't get out very much now because of your health.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, there's a time of year. But mostly, we're crazy over rocks, and we're rockhounds.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, yes, you are a rockhound. You and your husband both. And you enjoyed, for a long time, Sunday school work.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes. I love working with those kids. I just could hardly stand giving that up.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That's because of your health.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Because last year, I ended up with heart failure because I coughed so much. Yeah, I had broncholasm. And so this year, I just told them. I didn't want... I wasn't going to take it. And they said, we don't want you down here. We want you back alive. So I've been still going down from September up until last Sunday in December. I've been going to Sunday school. I had just automatically been down to this 4th, 5th, and 6th grade class. And I'm working right with them anyway. Until now, this month, I haven't been there. And she called me last Saturday morning. I was going in. I said no because I hadn't been out. I've tested her a lot. And she said, the kids ask about me. I don't... it's just so rewarding. I feel like this is something worthwhile. I really love it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And you've done it for how many years?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, at least 23 years.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So you've seen a lot of children grow up and go through Sunday school in this community, right?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: She was in Sunday school down here at Rockwood. Sunday school down here. Her mother and I worked together.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What do you do for recreation? That's an important question. I take an art class on Tuesdays and Fridays. In Potlatch? And I've been a 4A student for 10 years. I work at the school every week. I get to keep the kids. And I really enjoy that. You count that as recreation? Yes. It's most important to get away from...
